title: Void Ending in an Opposition to Neptune
source: Picatrix (adapted), Book I chapter 5, Book II chapter 3 and Book III chapter 1

<!-- generated by tools/content/gen-void.ts; edit the generator, not this file -->

The opposition is the hardest figure the Moon can close on: the text grades it as extreme enmity, because the signs it joins stand opposed across all four natural qualities. It shares with the square the warnings that guard every election, and a Moon waning in light and faced by Saturn is the source's own example of a serious misfortune.

When the Moon closes her course in a sign with an opposition to Neptune, the quiet stretch that follows carries something of his drifting mist. Neptune is unknown to Picatrix; the planet was found in 1846, by calculation before anyone saw it, and the source never mentions it. Any reading of it here is this almanac's extension of the lunar doctrine, not the doctrine itself. Named for the Greek lord of the sea, it is read as cold, blue, and dissolving: a course that closes on it ends in something misty, where edges soften and matters drift rather than conclude.
